speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government said that the recession is over. I would like to know: over for whom? Not for constituents in Northumberland, not for farmers across this land, not for fishermen, not for industry, small businesses, not for consumers. Very importantly, not for Canada's voiceless one million children living in poverty.
Poverty denies children and their families access to basic rights, access to food, clothing and adequate shelter. Childhood poverty translates into poor physical health, emotional trauma, poor educational achievements, early school drop-outs, and ultimately unskilled, uneducated, costly social assistance statistics.
Children in Canada and around the world deserve that basic rights be met. On September 30 last year our Prime Minister was co-chairman of the United Nations Summit for Children in New York which called for ratification of
a UN convention on the rights of the child. To date, 86 countries have ratified. Canada has not.
Ratification of the convention is an essential first step in fulfilling-
The hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, farmers will receive $1 billion less in income this year than they did last year. The solution of the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds is to tell farmers to dump a load of grain on the parking lots of European car dealerships and not to buy their products. The minister is apparently oblivious to the fact that farmers are not buying Mercedes-Benzes or BMWs these days.
Not only in western Canada but in Ontario as well thousands of producers are on the verge of losing a livelihood that took generations to build. Farm organizations from one end of the country to the other have been pointing out the need for a third line of defence payment. Why is the government ignoring its own program?
By the way, where are all the other programs that the PC government was going to introduce as part of the Growing Together paper it presented back in 1989?
Yes, the Europeans are causing problems for Canadian farmers, and yes, the Americans are causing problems for Canadian farmers.
If, however, the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds really wants to know the biggest problem Canadian farmers have today, he need only look in the mirror.

Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing that all Canadians can agree on, it is the need for Senate reform. What we cannot agree on is how to do it.

September 16, 1991
The 1979 Pepin-Robarts commission recommended that the Senate be replaced by a Council of Confederation, made up of delegations appointed by provincial governments based on representation by population. But a great many Canadians want a Triple-E Senate, one that is elected, equal, and effective.
Australia has a Triple-E senate as part of its federal parliamentary system of government. In Australia it works, not always smoothly and efficiently, but decisions are made and actions are taken.
Critics say that the Australian senate interferes with the government's right to govern, that is the cabinet's absolute control of the legislative process. Frankly, that may not be such a bad idea.

subtopic: NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR THE INTEGRATION OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR THE INTEGRATION OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity today to draw the attention of the House to the National Strategy for the Integration of Persons with Disabilities, which was adopted recently. As you know, the strategy was announced by the Prime Minister in Winnipeg on September 6.
Today, 3.3 million Canadians have a disability, and visible or not, the disability is very real for the person concerned.
These Canadians are not asking for special privileges. They are merely asking for equality.
Firmly resolved to respond to these legitimate concerns, the federal government has promised to spend $158 million to support this national strategy and its three objectives: equal access, economic integration and full participation.
The federal government wants to make it possible for persons with disabilities to take an active part in the economic and social life of this country.
Mr. Speaker, together we can build a Canada where all citizens will have-

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are very upset and frustrated about the GST, income taxes, unemployment and drug use. In metro Toronto the issue of drug use is of concern to parents in almost every neighbourhood.
This problem must be tackled through the education of youth and through effective police enforcement programs. The federal government has been asked repeatedly by Toronto metro council and metro police commission that part of the money the metro police force uses in pursuing drug investigations, and a share of the value of property and proceeds confiscated by the RCMP, be returned to metro authorities to be spent on education, crime prevention, rehabilitation programs and anti-drug enforcement activities.
Once again we urge the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General to support the fight against drugs on the streets and in the schools by acceding to these very reasonable requests.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in June 1990 an all-party committee of this House under the capable chairmanship of the hon. member for Oxford tabled a report called A Consensus For Action. The report outlined barriers that prevent the full participation of Canadians with disabilities in the daily life of our country. I was frankly cynical as to whether anything substantive would come from the report and its recommendations.
Accordingly, I was delighted and would like to commend the Prime Minister and the government for their important announcement of the national strategy for the integration of persons with disabilities. Furthermore, the strategy includes a tangible commitment of $158 million.
Canadians with disabilities are not asking for special privileges. They merely ask for equitable treatment and the same opportunity and access to fulfil their lives and to make their contribution to Canada as are enjoyed by other Canadians.
September 16, 1991

This government's announcement and its strategy is one more important step in this direction.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to publicly thank the Public Service Alliance of Canada and its members for agreeing to work behind their own picket lines in order to participate in the B.C. Salmon Hatchery Egg Take Program.
This action has saved a precious and valuable resource from certain extinction in areas around the 17 major hatcheries in British Columbia.
The Conservative government was prepared to see the west coast salmon resource go down the drain with everything else it has touched in this country. Thanks to the Public Service Alliance of Canada, which put the interests of the public and future generations first, this valuable resource has been saved. Thanks to the Public Service Alliance of Canada and its members, this is one precious resource that will not be destroyed by the Mulroney government.

Mr. Speaker, the agriculture industry is once again suffering. This time it is not an act of God but the actions of the grain handlers and the longshoremen's union. The grain handlers have chosen to support the Public Service strike, thus disrupting the very industry that feeds them and their families.
This type of action cannot be condoned or tolerated. Agriculture is essential to the economic prosperity of this country and should be declared accordingly. Legislation must be put in place to secure the well-being of the agri-food industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the thousands of college and university students returning to school this month have little to cheer about. Many failed to secure work this summer in Canada's depressed economy. Now the neediest of these students, those who have applied for
financial assistance through the Canada Student Loans Program, realize as they go to cash their cheques that they must pay up front 3 per cent of their assistance as an administration fee.
Shame on this federal government. Not only has it made post-secondary education more expensive and exclusive through its cuts to education transfers, but now it purports to tax one of the most important programs that help our youth pay these soaring costs.
To add yet another obstacle to accessible education, this government has chosen to close its campus employment centres, thus eliminating another important avenue for paying for an education, a job.
Mr. Speaker, when will this government stop starving and start investing in education in this country?

Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of the strike by the Public Service Alliance of Canada, the Leader of the Bloc Quebecois has remained silent. The reason is this: On May 24, 1991, in Le Soleil, Mr. Denis Gagne, a member of the teachers' union in Chicoutimi, reported the following: "In 1982-83, Lucien Bouchard represented the PQ government on the employer's side during negotiations with the public and semi-public sector".
According to Mr. Gagne, in addition to his income from his law firm in Chicoutimi, Mr. Bouchard was paid more than $250,000 by the Quebec government to introduce a 20 per cent cut in the salaries of teachers, nurses and all social sector employees in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, thousands of striking public servants came to Parliament Hill today. When they left an hour later, the lawns of this public building were a sea of trash-placards deliberately shredded into small pieces and ground into the grass.

Mr. Speaker, this is not a big deal, but it is symbolic and it is very distressing. I do not know what goal the union bosses, egged on by the Leader of the NDP, were trying to accomplish through this eco-violence, but for those Canadians who travelled here to see their Parliament Buildings, this was a disgrace. Surely the strikers do not have an argument with the lawn of the House of Commons. If the union's friends in the NDP cannot teach them to respect Parliament, at least they can tell them it is wrong to wantonly harm the environment.

Mr. Speaker, the first general strike in the Public Service in Canada's history is the result of the unfair and dictatorial tactics of this government.
By suspending collective bargaining and refusing to negotiate equitable wage conditions, the Conservative government has destroyed the co-operation that must exist between public service management and employees if essential services are to be provided to the Canadian public.

In the National Capital Region, the economic effects of this strike are being felt in the business community. Local television news broadcasts reported that my riding of Carleton-Gloucester was suffering severely from the negative effects of the loss of the revenue normally generated by public servants.
I call upon the government to act with fairness by respecting the fundamental right of its employees to a fair and just contract.

Mr. Speaker, the Public Service Alliance of Canada has taken extraordinary steps to promote its cause. In my riding, the union hierarchy has resorted to bringing in professional agitators and union extremists to take the place of local PSAC members who refuse to walk the line.
If they had a choice, they would prefer not to strike. This is not peculiar to my riding, it is happening across
the country. The use of professional agitators and extremists to enforce a picket only brings the reputation of the labour movement into disrepute.
I call upon the PSAC to refrain from this type of tactic.

Mr. Speaker, in 1977 the Liberals brought in pay equity legislation, but they never moved on it. In the 1984 throne speech, this government promised pay equity for its underpaid women workers. During the 1988 leaders' debate, the Prime Minister said: "We are agreeing on a policy for pay equity for women. We are budgeting for the funds required on an ongoing basis."
Now the government sings a different tune. The Tories are saying no deal to women working for $19,000 a year. They have tried twice to stop the Canadian Human Rights Commission from looking at pay equity in the Public Service. The Human Rights Commissioner has said that the government is not playing fair on pay equity. Shame on this government, Mr. Speaker. Where are those funds that were budgeted? Why have cabinet ministers and their friends received increases and not women workers at the lower end of the economic pay scale?

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all hon. members, I want to offer congratulations to the Minister of Veterans Affairs on his being honoured this morning for his work on behalf of Canadian veterans and their families.
The National Council of Veterans Associations this morning presented the minister with its prestigious medal of service. Also this morning, the national vicepresident of the Korean Veterans Association presented the Minister of Veterans Affairs with an honorary life membership. In presenting the medal of service Cliff Chadderton, the chairman of the National Council, said: "Geriy Merrithew is not only a good Minister of Veterans Affairs, he has shown himself as well to be a great Canadian and must be given credit for the current efforts being made by veterans' organizations to preserve our national unity".
September 16, 1991

Canada's programs for veterans are second to none. The same can be said for the minister who leads and directs those programs.

Mr. Speaker, September 7 marked an historic milestone in Canada's history. One hundred years ago, Wasyl Eleniak and Ivan Pylipiw entered Canada and were the first of the Ukrainian immigrants to settle in the prairies to link our country from sea to sea.
These pioneers struggled against disease, poverty, climate and social indignities. They fought hard, persevered and succeeded. In the years that followed their community has given Canada successful farmers, educators, entrepreneurs, mayors, MLAs, members of Parliament and the Senate, a justice of the Supreme Court of Canada and a Governor General.
Such is the success of the Ukrainian community that immigrants and new citizens of today look at their story of struggle and success as a model to follow.
It has been said that Canada's true wealth stems from its citizens. Let it also be said that all Canadians are proud of the Ukrainian presence in its citizenry. Indeed the Ukrainian Canadian centennial is about all of us. I therefore urge Parliament and this government to continue to give attention to this year-long celebration, not only in the interest of cultural equality but also for the sake of national unity.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are back in Parliament. We would like to have started in an easier fashion because this country needs some order, but unfortunately, there is a terrible strike that nobody wants, including the strikers.
A few minutes ago the Public Service Staff Relations Board-I talked with the president and it was confirmed to me-ruled that this government is not respecting the
Oral Questions
law of the land and is in breach of section 51 of the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
Will the Prime Minister do the right thing at this moment, follow the law of the land, go back to the negotiation table and try to find a solution to this unfair situation that exists today whereby the poorest in the Public Service are receiving a zero increase in their pay when people in the higher echelons are getting a big pay increase?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put to rest once and for all the notion that higher civil servants are supposed to be getting treatment that others will not get. This is not the truth. This is not a fact.
The civil servant upper echelon managers will all go through the same system of zero, three and three, as you will be going through and as we will be going through.
As a matter of fact, we negotiated a settlement for our managers from June 1990 to June 1991. A commission set up by the Liberal Party recommended 6.2 per cent. I refused it for last year. I settled for 4.2, which is less than what PS AC got. As of June this year they were already at zero increase.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that we want to find a solution and that we want to start this session in an orderly fashion, since it will be a very important one for Canada. That being said, perhaps the government could start this session by respecting the laws of this country. A few minutes ago, a federal board, established by an Act of Parliament, said that this government had violated Section 51. Does the minister intend to observe the laws of this country and go back to the bargaining table to find a way to resolve this dispute?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning, the Public Service Staff Relations Board answered two questions from the union. The first question was: Did the government-and I am quoting the union-bargain in bad faith? The Board did not agree. However, it did say that in its opinion, we probably should have made every reasonable effort to reach an agreement.

Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition may not be aware of the fact that we have been negotiating with the Public Service Alliance of Canada for seven months, and that, give or take a few hours, we have had 60 days of bargaining and 30 days of conciliation. I had a meeting with Mr. Bean Friday morning, and he said he would never accept the government's policy. We were prepared to negotiate all terms of the collective agreement, except for the budgetary policy related 0-3, and he refused.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everyone in this land understands that the intention of this government was to have a strike. It has been working all this time to make sure there is a strike which will serve its political purposes.
I want to ask the minister if he will do the right thing. The people of Canada are suffering today. They want an end to this strike. A very easy way to solve this problem is to appoint a mediator who will have the right to look at all the problems. The public servants will go back to work and we will have peace in this country. Then we will be able to deal with the other fantastic problems of this nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
I see that the Leader of the Opposition has another miracle solution. I do not know if it is the same as the one he had yesterday which was rejected by the unions.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, at budget time we made many difficult decisions. One was related to the union. This is not union bashing because many unions have accepted the 0-3 and have signed agreements with us. We have negotiated in good faith. We have conciliation board reports recommending acceptance.
What we wanted to do at budget time and we are doing today is making sure that the debt does not go up and the deficit does not go up, but that interest rates go down and inflation goes down, and it is working, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, this government has dealt in bad faith with seniors, with the unemployed, with students, with farmers and fishermen and now it is dealing in bad faith with its own employees.
Canadians understand what good faith means. When is this government going to recognize that it is in violation of the law of this Parliament? What is it going to do to put itself in conformity with the law as every other Canadian citizen has to do?
Respect the law.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course we respect the law. I will look at the report which was handed to me just before Question Period.
I will say this. The best way to provide for a secure future for our public servants and for all Canadians is to be really helpful and not to go about making statements such as that we are determined to hit the unions or to hit the Public Service. This is not true at all. We are determined to help them by getting the finances of this country in order and out of the mess that existed when your party was in power and we are having some success. Would they prefer the Liberal way with interest rates of 22 per cent and with inflation at 14 per cent? I think they prefer our answer to those questions.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Canadians understand belt-tightening, they understand fairness and they also understand obeying the law, which 99 per cent of them do. The board has clearly found this government in violation of the law of Parliament. I ask again, what will the government do to get back to the bargaining table and negotiate fairly, in accordance with the law, and stop the turmoil it has caused in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to tell the hon. member that I am ready to meet with Daryl Bean any time he wants-this afternoon, if he so chooses. But I want it to be very clear that we are not moving from the zero and three, but we are prepared to-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
This is not something new. It was in the budget. If the Liberals are so worried about the legislated wage freeze, what did they say about the premier of New Brunswick-your province, Mr. Leader of the Opposition-when he legislated a freeze of 0 per cent?

We are going through a difficult period. We are making decisions, we are not passing them on to our children.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister, because it seems clear from the minister's answers that he does not understand the difference between negotiating and dictating.
Independent conciliation boards have said that this government must bargain in good faith and has not been doing so. The Staff Relations Board again this afternoon made the same judgment and said the government was not complying with section 51 of the act. There is only one group in this dispute which is acting in good faith and that is the Public Service Alliance, which today said that to show good faith they would take down the pickets at airports and they would expedite border crossings.
Will the Prime Minister show good faith and instruct his government's negotiators to sit down now with public servants who do so much good work for this country, negotiate in good faith and negotiate on the terms of the contract on which they are entitled to negotiate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to negotiate in good faith one has to take account of the reality of life.
Would the Leader of the NDP propose that I use the Daryl Bean solution? When he was faced with similar problems a few months ago he said: "I understand that my staff members are a little bitter and frustrated, but these are tough times", and he proceeded to close 20 positions.
I prefer to keep our civil servants and to give them an offer which on the whole is reasonable.

Mr. Speaker, public servants know perfectly well what is happening. This year, for instance, a speech writer working for one of the government's ministers was paid nearly $24,000 for five weeks of work. Meanwhile, some 5,000 public service employees, most of them women, earn about $20,000 a year, for 52 weeks.
My question is directed to the Prime Minister. Everyone says that wage equity is a matter of simple justice.
Oral Questions
Why won't this government do the right thing now for women, for the most disadvantaged members of the Public Service?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party mentioned the problems experienced by public servants in this situation, and as someone who has been a public servant for much of his life, I must say I understand the problem.
However, I think they also realize what the situation is and that today, in all sectors, collective agreements are being renegotiated. What about Canadian Airlines and Air Canada? We are going through a difficult period, and these are the people who will have to pay, with their salaries.
I understand why public servants are upset. They deserve to get a lot more. But that being said, as far as equity is concerned, it is a very serious problem and we are constantly looking for ways to improve the situation in this country.
I think the Leader of the NDP could at least acknowledge the initiative taken by this government in 1990 to set aside $317 million to bring wages to equitable levels, and that same government is adding $87 million annually. I think that is quite something, considering the present financial situation. I agree there is room for improvement, and we are prepared to make those improvements.

Mr. Speaker, I would like the people of Canada to understand that the Canadian Human Rights Commission, which said that this government must institute pay equity, is being taken to court and challenged by this government about pay equity. The people of Canada and the women of Canada understand that.
We have a situation here where senior management, senior civil servants and indeed members of Parliament are receiving salary increases. We see the head of the Bank of Canada receiving a substantial increase. We have received a substantial increase this year.

Oral Questions
Oh, oh.
I ask the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party to put her question.

I want to simply ask the Prime Minister a question.
On one hand, we do have those who are the most privileged in our society receiving salary increases. On the other hand, we have people who are working for the Public Service, such as single parents, women, still making $20,000 a year. This government says no to them. Is this right? Or is this wrong?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not right and it is certainly not true.
I will repeat again that the senior managers of the Canadian government, the ministers, the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the members of Parliament will all receive when the time comes at the first of December, zero per cent for the following year. They will receive 3 per cent the year after and 3 per cent the year after that.
Members of Parliament will not get an increase before January 1, 1933.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: With regard to the managers, the year starts in June. The Alliance got 4.8 per cent and the managers got 4.2 per cent for last year. Since June, they are at zero per cent increase.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: I wish the leader would get her facts straight.

Mr. Speaker, if it is 1933, maybe the minister will make it retroactive.
I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries who has had in his hot little hands for two months now a report stating in graphic detail that the Newfoundland inshore fishery is in absolute total collapse.
For example, 8,200 fishermen and plant workers on the northeast coast alone, including some in his riding, will not qualify this year for UI although all of them qualified last year.
Is the minister now ready to act on the recommendations in that report and bring in an aid package for those fishermen and plant workers, or some sort of a catch failure program?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that the fishery along the northeast coast of Newfoundland and along the coast of Labrador has been extremely poor this year due, one has to assume, to very late ice conditions, cold and sloppy water and to the fact that as a result of that the codfish and the capelin have not come in as they normally do.
There has been an absolute, total collapse in certain areas such as for example the fishery in Labrador. It would not be true to say that there has been an absolute total collapse of the inshore fishery in Newfoundland this year, but there is a serious situation with respect to the northeast coast.
It is likely that the amount of inshore cod caught along that coast this year might only be 50 per cent of what it was last year. We do have a serious situation. This has been under assessment now for some weeks. We are considering with the provincial government-
Answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: If this is unimportant to the hon. gentleman opposite, I can sit down. We have been consult' with the Government of Newfoundland and wit. me industry there for some time. We will be bringing forward proposals when they are ready.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the minister it is due to ice and sloppy water, but I think he might agree it is due to some fairly sloppy government as well.
These fishermen and these plant workers, as he knows, have no fish, no money, and what is now painfully obvious is that they have nobody in the cabinet prepared to argue, to plead the urgency of their particular case.
Why is the minister dragging his feet on this? Why does he not take off that St. John's fish merchants hat and go to bat for those people who are really hurting out there and who, contrary to what he says, are caught in situation of total collapse in the fishery? He should check his figures because they are much more dramatic than he would admit in this House.
September 16, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will leave it up to the viewing audience to judge the grossness of this rhetoric, but I would just point out that when the fishermen along this coast needed assistance from May and, in fact, well up in August with respect to the fact they could not fish because of ice, I arranged a nice compensation program that has put $18 million into their hands during that period.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture who knows that farmers right across this country, grain and oilseeds, horticulture producers, are facing the worst financial crisis in a generation because the government has not provided emergency transitional funding for the losses in last year's crop.
I want to ask the minister when this government is going to act. When are they going to provide this assistance in view of the tremendous disaster facing Canadian producers this summer.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, assistance provided by the Government of Canada and the provincial governments last year was assistance to bring us forward to this time where the safety net programs, both GRIP and NISA, could be put in place.
I remind the hon. member that both GRIP and NISA were designed by farm groups, by provincial governments, and by the Government of Canada. It was at the request of the farmers and their organizations that there be a very specific support system in place. That is what we have at this time, and as we proceed with the interim payments on GRIP, and with the NISA payments that are going out at this time, the producers will receive the support that the hon. member is asking for. These programs were designed in co-operation with producers.
I understand this is a difficult time, but as the cash flow of some $2 billion from these safety net programs enters
Oral Questions
the farmers' hands, they will find that it has been this government and the provincial governments that have come to their support in this time of low prices.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows that his own third line of defence emergency committee rejected that solution two weeks ago in Winnipeg. They told him and asked him to provide emergency assistance, third line of defence based on the losses that occurred in the past crop year.
I want' to ask the minister when he is going to recognize that they have made a mistake and that they have to bring forth emergency assistance for those losses as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member should recognize is that the Farm Support and Adjustment Measures, FSAM, that were put in place this summer totalled over $650 million. Those support systems were put in place to bridge farmers into the safety nets for the 1991 crop. Farmers are now concluding this crop. They will then be able to apply under the GRIP and NISA programs.
I say to the hon. member with all sincerity that if he wishes to support the grains and oilseed sector, if he wishes to support the cattle industry and other important agriculture sectors, he will support this government in getting the grain moving, opening up the packing plants, allowing producers access to a market that is being denied because of the PSAC strike.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture who surely knows that we can deliver all the $2 wheat we like and we will never get ourselves out of the hole that farmers are in as a result of last year's shortfall of income. It is that last year's shortfall of more than $1 billion that is not being addressed by this government. GRIP and NISA address this coming year. They cannot carry that deficit into a year with $2 wheat which has less purchasing power than was ever the case in the history of recorded wheat prices.
What happened to the third line of defence payment? What became of the third line of defence? It was promised throughout the negotiations all of last year and it has disappeared. What happened to it?

September 16, 1991
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member or at least I really believe the hon. member is not saying that the some $650 million that was put forward on the third line of defence to bring the grains and oilseed producers over into the safety nets of GRIP and NISA is nothing.
That is not enough.

One member from the Liberal Party says that is not enough. I understand that it is difficult at this time, but I remind colleagues that the third line of defence committee met in September in Winnipeg, addressed this issue and recognized that the very system the hon. member is criticizing is a system that was identified by producers, the provincial government and the Government of Canada to assist grains and oilseeds producers through this very difficult time, until stabilization through GRIP and NISA can be achieved.

Mr. Speaker, the minister will recognize that throughout the negotiations it was understood by all of the negotiating parties that third line of defence would apply for those periods of time when GRIP and NISA were not in effect, which is namely the crop year that has just finished.
When is the government going to make the third line of defence an effective program, rather than introducing red herrings such as was produced in April which reduced the premiums that were expenses farmers did not have before GRIP and NISA were introduced? When will it address the real problem of a shortfall of $1 billion?

Mr. Speaker, as part of the assistance through this bridging process there was assistance provided by the Government of Canada on the premium of 25 per cent for the gross revenue insurance program.

Some would say, though, that he was probably happiest jogging daily at 90 years of age and urging, by his example, an entire and sometimes reluctant nation to follow his route to good health and longevity.

When he was the Governor General-

Mr. Michener led a life we can all be proud of. After serving in this House as a member, he went on to become the Speaker of the House of Commons, Canadian ambassador to India and Governor General of Canada. He served his country well. He did so with unequalled dedication and enthousiasm.

Roland Michener was, to most of us, much more than a Rhodes scholar and admired House of Commons Speaker. The core of his character represented so much to us about what is good about Canada. His tolerance and his understanding, his sense of fairness and in fact his sense of humour were something that immediately attracted all Canadians and we too became part of that mission that he had on behalf of Canada.
Finally, I would like to say that Roland Michener led a very colourful and productive life. I am sure all of us hope that the values that he stood for and the love that he had for his country will live on in all of us.
THE LATE SENATOR AZELLUS DENIS [Translation]

Mr. Speaker, when the time comes to pay a final tribute to a man who gave 56 years of his life to politics, I realize that few of my fellow citizens meet the definition of "political" as clearly as Azellus Denis did.
It can be said that by practising for more than half a century a profession that he loved, he acquired virtues like realism, prudence and a certain wisdom that arose from this long experience. For if the scholar studies books, as Balzac said, the politician studies people, their interests and the causes that give rise to their actions. Shrewd, sensible, at times crafty, Senator Denis, who had been a member of Parliament for 28 years, was a real politician. Political institutions-organization, government and public affairs-had long ceased to hold secrets for him.

September 16, 1991
Tributes
I can even say that he was what is called a "political animal", that is, someone with all the talents and all the shrewdness required to work effectively as a zealous member of his party.
Allow me a few moments more for a career which will go down in the annals of the Commonwealth as-

-probably one of those who served the longest in the Commonwealth, 56 years: 28 as a member and 28 as a senator.

Under an often rough exterior, the man whom everyone affectionately called Azellus, sometimes with a hint of mockery, had a tender heart. Ele had a sense for friendship; he had the gift of keeping his friends. It is regrettable that he refused to write his memoirs, despite my many requests.
Fortunately, I remember very well our many meetings and discussions, from the first day I was his master of ceremonies in 1949.
Mr. Speaker, you can imagine what this politician, who knew the end of the Great Depression when he was first elected in 1935, who knew the Second World War, who knew conscription, who knew the glorious post-war years, who witnessed the establishment of NATO, would have had to say to us. He was always loyal to his party. He served Mackenzie King, of whom he spoke to us so often, and was elected with him in 1940 and 1945. In 1948 came the great and friendly Louis Saint-Laurent, reelected with him in 1949, 1953 and 1957. As he said, while his party was defeated, he was re-elected.
Then there was Lester B. Pearson, the fine and distinguished diplomat. He was re-elected with him in 1958, a very difficult year for us, and witnessed the end of the Diefenbaker regime in 1962 as well as the coming to power of Pearson in 1963. I am getting now to the most important part of his life. He, the man who understood the poor so well, was made Minister of Postal Services. No doubt the popularity he enjoyed at the time would have been of great help today. In 1964, he was appointed
to the Senate, where he sat ever since, and I had the privilege of taking over as member for his former riding.
Imagine how much I learned from him about the Duplessis era and the turbulent and exhilarating days of debate on the Quiet Revolution! He was a first class member of Parliament-and I am addressing those who are listening as well as those who should-great at representing his riding, always available to his people, to the little man and the less affluent members of society.
This is something we should reflect upon at this time, Mr. Speaker. It is unfortunate that you did not have the opportunity of hearing him in caucus when he stood up for the needy in a style of his own, of course, and without all the usual media fanfare. He was a reserved, quiet and modest man of good advice on people and on things.
Someone wrote about on him, on the role he played in Rene Levesque's election in 1960.
Having been close to the action in those days, I can assure you that, had it not been for him and my late father, Rene Levesque would have never made it in 1960, and you can read about this in Rene Levesque's memoirs.
A man of wisdom with a colourful way of expressing himself, with his demise, another page of parliamentary history is turned. To his wife, my dear friend, Mrs. Eme Denis, I extend, on behalf of us all, my best wishes for a long life and the assurance that today we are with her in our prayers. Have no fear, honourable colleagues, Azellus was welcomed in Paradise by his many friends, always anxious to know what is going on down here, on this troubled earth and in this party he loved so dearly.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join the hon. member for Saint-Denis and the Minister of National Defence in offering my sincere condolences to the family of Senator Denis.

He was in this House with us for many years and was another example of a person who decided to serve. All of his life he was involved in organizations that meant something to the grassroots, such as the Red Cross and organizations of this nature. Later, when he came to this Parliament, he was always trying to be a bridge between the different factions in this House. He was always involved in interparliamentary organizations, very often travelling abroad.
He was an anglophone who was extremely proud of the fact that he would participate in organizations of members of Parliament in the French language. For him it was a great contribution.
I had the privilege of working with him when he was my parliamentary secretary in 1980 when we were involved in the referendum and patriation of the Constitution. Whenever I felt the pressure, Ken was there
Tributes
giving me a good slap on the back and telling me to keep up the good work. He will be missed.
I see his wife and his two sons in the gallery. You have to be proud of your husband and your father. He was a great guy and we will miss him very much.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I too want to say how saddened we were when we learned last Wednesday of the passing of Senator Denis.
Senator Denis served in Parliament for more than half a century. He was elected before many of us were bom.
While I do not have knowledge of what happens inside the Liberal caucus, I do know from various comments that people have made over the years, that when discussions of a critical nature occurred, Senator Denis often stood back, but when he did speak, he spoke for the people. When we look at Senator Denis' record and acknowledge the fact that he was first elected in 1935, re-elected in 1940, 1945, 1949, 1953, 1957, 1958, 1962, 1963, you know that here was an individual who not only served his constituents well, but served his country well.
Mr. Speaker, our prayers and our sympathies go out to his fine wife.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to add a few words, especially after what was said by our colleage from Saint-Denis. I know Senator Denis was his political mentor, and I also happen to know the Senator was an important factor in the political career of the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel.
Personally, as someone who met Senator Denis, first as a ministerial assistant and later as a member of this House, I can testify to the fact that he was genuine. When we say French Canadian, with all that traditionally implies, Senator Denis was a real French Canadian. I heard him speak over the years, and what he said was always imbued with common sense. We have all had occasion to listen to his remarks, and today, with my colleagues, I wish to pay tribute to the senator and thank him for his words of wisdom and his advice were greatly appreciated.

THE LATE WILLIAM KENNETH ROBINSON [English]

Mr. Speaker, it was with sadness that we learned about the passing of our former colleague, William Kenneth Robinson, former member of Parliament for Etobicoke-Lakeshore. Ken Robinson suffered from a brain tumour and died at the Queensway General Hospital on July 25 when this House was not sitting.
As our leader has already said, he is survived by his wife Margery and his two sons, John and James, brothers Keith, Arthur, Norman and sisters Verna Tanner and Shirley Mathews.
Ken Robinson represented the Etobicoke-Lakeshore riding for 14 years, from 1968 to 1972 and again from 1974 to 1984. In 1984 his political career was cut short when, on the evening of his own nomination, he ended up in hospital.
Ken was a hard worker and liked the challenge. He talked to me a lot about his responsibilities as parliamentary secretary to four ministers, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General, the Minister of State for Social Development, the Minister of National Revenue. He served conscientiously on two parliamentary standing committees, the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs and the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. He was an active member on the international unions and associations, the Interparliamentary Union, known as IPU; the Canadian Native Parliamentary Union; the Canadian Parliamentary Helsinki Group; the Canada-U.S. Inter-Parliamentary Group, and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.
Ken received his law degree from Osgoode Hall and practised in his own law firm in Etobicoke as Queen's Counsel. I learned from his family today that Ken was a lifetime learner and just last year he received his doctorate in philosophy.
Mr. Speaker, if you check the Canadian Parliamentary Guide you will see that Mr. Robinson probably held the Guiness Book of World Records for belonging to various associations, societies and organizations. He served with the Royal Canadian Air Force and was a lieutenant-colonel in the reserves. He was honorary president of the St. John's Ambulance Association, a member of the Board of Governors of Queensway General Hospital Association. He was on the Metropolitan Toronto Social Planning Council; president of the Canadian Tai Kwan Do Association; patron of the Canadian Field Hockey Association; chairman of the Gurkha Welfare Trust Canada.
Ken was also active in the Etobicoke-Queensway Lions Club, where memorial services will be held on October 11,1991 at 8 p.m. This memorial service is being organized by the residents of Etobicoke and West Toronto, again indicating their appreciation for what Ken did for his community and for the country.
Ken was a member of the Royal Canadian Legion, Branch 217; he was a member of the John Howard Society, the Elizabeth Fry Society. He was also a member of the Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto, the Association of Corrections and Criminology, the Canadian Club, the UN Association in Canada, the Royal Commonwealth Society, the Canadian branch of Amnesty International, and that is just a bit of what is listed in the Canadian Parliamentary Guide.
Ken had a big heart. He was always ready to help others, whether it was helping others through his parliamentary role, his law profession, through the Liberal Party or through his day to day activities. Ken was a well-liked workaholic, putting in long hours and eight-day work weeks. It was not uncommon to see Ken in his office at 11 p.m. or midnight or even 1 o'clock in the morning. He will be missed by his family, colleagues in this House, his friends and, above all, his constituents. Ken represented his constituents for 14 years, the constituents of Etobicoke-Lakeshore.

I rise today on behalf of the members of this side to pay tribute to Colonel Ken Robinson. I might start by saying, sir, that the current member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore, Mr. Patrick Boyer, wanted to be here specifically to do this himself but, like Wayne Gretzky, he has back problems this week and cannot be here. He sends his personal regrets and homage.
To know Ken was to know a very special guy. I had the privilege, sir, of knowing him in this House and outside this House. Not only did we spend four years here together in parliamentary service, but we served for many years on the councils both locally and nationally of the Royal Commonwealth Society, which is only one-as my colleague has indicated-of the dozens of important national institutions to which Ken gave unstintingly of his time and his energy.
September 16, 1991

To know Ken was to know one of the proudest Canadians one could ever meet. No Canadian, English or French speaking ever fought harder in the defence of his or her heritage. His record of public service and dedication will serve as a shining example to all of us.
On behalf of all the members on this side, sir, we extend our sincere condolences to his wife Margery, and his two sons, Jamie and John.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party caucus, I want to say how saddened we were when we heard the news on July 25 of the passing of Ken Robinson.
My colleagues in the House of Commons have commented on the wide range of ways in which Ken served his community and his country. In the Canadian Parliamentary Guide, Mr. Speaker, it goes on longer than almost any other parliamentarian, listing all of the ways Ken served his country.

I will be forever grateful for the generosity he showed me during those novice years as a parliamentarian.
Our hearts go out to an individual who served this country with distinction, who was an extremely hardworking parliamentarian on behalf of his party and the House of Commons and, in particular, on behalf of his constituents.
Our prayers and our thoughts today are with his wife Margery and his two sons Jamie and John.

Mr. Speaker, it is a real privilege and honour today to speak on behalf of the Conservative Party of Canada in honour of Mrs. Grace Maclnnis who passed away this summer at the age of 85 in Sechelt, British Columbia.
We understand that during her last years she suffered greatly from arthritis, but this physical affliction did not affect her in any way mentally. She was noted when she was a member of this House, as well as the provincial legislature, for her keen mind, the strong and well reasoned positions that she took on matters she felt were important to her.
As I mentioned, she served as an MLA in the provincial legislature from 1941 to 1945 for the riding of Vancouver-Burrard and served as the member of Parliament for Vancouver East from 1965 to 1972. This was a seat that her husband Angus had held previously from 1935 to 1957.

September 16, 1991
Tributes
I might add that my grandfather was a very strong advocate of the CCF party at that time and a good friend of the Maclnnises. Like Mr. Woodsworth, he would spend half his time preaching the gospel and half the time preaching the gospel of socialism.
Mrs. Maclnnis was elected as a member of Parliament from British Columbia. She was also the only woman member of Parliament when she was here in the House. She was involved in issues which were not popular at that time such as contraception and abortion. She took her stand and her position, for which I understand she was ridiculed roundly by her male colleagues. She also undertook a stand on the humane treatment for the Japanese internees during the war, again a position that was not popular.
As I said, she was a woman of keen intellect, great principles and determination. I am sure that she will be missed by all her friends and colleagues but she has left each one of us a pioneering legacy not only as Canadians but as parliamentarians. So we wish her survivors and her colleagues the best wishes that we possibly can at this sad time.

Mr. Speaker, I also rise to pay tribute to Grace Maclnnis who died on July 17, 1991. Grace Maclnnis, the MP for Vancouver Kingsway from 1965 to 1972, was an outstanding Canadian. She was a charter member of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation which was founded by her father, J. S. Woodsworth, in 1933.
As my colleague said, she represented Vancouver Burrard in Victoria from 1941 to 1945 and was the first woman from British Columbia to become a member of Parliament in 1965. She was married to Angus Maclnnis, who had earlier represented Vancouver East for 22 years, and she carried on his fight for redress for Japanese Canadians.
Grace Maclnnis represented all that is best in a politician and a member of Parliament. She had clear goals as a democratic socialist, a deep respect for people, and a dogged determination to fight for what she believed was right. She spoke eloquently about bread and butter issues that affected peoples' lives, encouraging people to organize and take collective action to solve problems and work for change.
She did not hesitate to speak her mind. She was bilingual and had a strong appreciation of Quebec's place in Canada.
I knew Grace personally best on the front lines of community action in the 1970s when she encouraged public housing tenants and mothers on welfare to organize and fight for their rights to child care, jobs, decent housing, and a say in decisions that affected their lives.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall how she brought their cause to Parliament and spoke up for them.
Women parliamentarians will appreciate that Grace Maclnnis had a lonely life as the only female member of Parliament in 1968. Despite the heckling from male colleagues who she once referred to as "MCPs", she continued to fight for birth control programs and the right to choice on abortion. She often said that all children should be wanted and loved and women should make their own decisions on medical matters. She advocated pay for parenting so women would not have to suffer the indignities of welfare and their essential work would be recognized.
After retirement, Grace continued her interest in people and Canada and in our party. Despite failing health, she was in demand as an inspirational speaker and she rarely refused an invitation. Painfully crippled with arthritis, she used to say: "I work fine from the neck up".
She continued to be an inspiration for aspiring politicians, including several of us in the House, and a role model for women across Canada. Above all, Grace Maclnnis cared for children and wanted a better world for future generations. She established the Lucie L. Woodsworth fund in memory of her mother to enrich the lives of disadvantaged children.
Grace Maclnnis will remain an inspiration to future generations for her pioneering efforts in the CCF-NDP, her integrity as a politician, her love of Canada, and her dedication to achieving a peaceful and caring world through social democracy.
On behalf of members of Parliament, I extend condolences to her family and friends in their loss. We also celebrate her rich life that has left a legacy for all of us.

Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH AND WELFARE, SOCIAL AFFAIRS AND THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this earliest reasonable opportunity as the House reconvenes today to rise and speak to the question of privilege raised by the member for Surrey North at 1500 hours on June 19, shortly before the House adjourned that evening for the summer. Unlike the said hon. member who failed to give me notice when he spoke at that time, due notice of my intention to now rise and respond has been given not only to the Chair but also to him.
To rationalize his claim that his personal privileges as a member of this House were breached, the member for Surrey North made three serious allegations to which I will respond point by point in this Chamber as well. First, he claimed that I prematurely released parts of the June 1991 first report of the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare, Social Affairs and the Status of Women, henceforth entitled Health Care System in Canada and its Funding: No Easy Solutions, prior to it being tabled in this House later that afternoon at about 1700 hours.

Privilege
I would like to inform the House that I did not release any copy, in full or in part, of the aforementioned final report; in fact, I first saw the final report after it was tabled. Neither did I release, in whole or in part, any of the draft reports despite requests by a reporter for a copy. I did, however, discuss the central thrust and message of the report with a reporter when interviewed by phone. I have since noted in the media clipping of June 19 that four of eight recommendations out of the 40 in the final report had nearly the same wording as when finally reported.
I must call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that the central thrust of the information I shared with the media has been in the public domain for quite some time, either as recommendations of the many witnesses who appeared before the standing committee on health and welfare since the study was initiated in the previous Parliament or as two interim reports by the committee, the first tabled in this House on September 13, 1988 and the second on June 18, 1990 of the present Parliament. These interim reports summarize "recurring themes in the briefs and testimony of witnesses".
Nevertheless, I have since realized that I might have exceeded my enthusiasm and might have shared with the public far more of the central themes than I would wish before its tabling in this House. For this, Mr. Speaker, I apologize in case I hurt this institution of Parliament.
Second, the member for Surrey North also alleged that I misrepresented the contents of the report when I told the press: "all parties have given their support to the report".
Third, he alleged that I knew the New Democratic Party and he did not support the majority report and that I knew he "had voted against the report" and therefore I misrepresented his position. These are simply not true. Conceivably the member could even use for his defence Appendix F. I will therefore speak to it very briefly.
Appendix F, subtitled Minority Report and seen on page 113 of the whole report clearly states in the second sentence of the opening paragraph:
While I would concur with many recommendations in the report,
I do dissent with the report in the following areas.
And he indicated the two areas he purported gave dissenting opinions. While Appendix F suggests absence of concurrence, even this claim on his part disappears under careful scrutiny.
I wish I could examine more fully for the House today his dissenting opinions and recommendations against recommendation nos. 1, 3, 12,17, 28,30, 37 and 39, which I have called to the attention of the Speaker when I gave notice that I would not go through that in the interest of time.
I would, however, just like to cite two short examples. In the minority report-and I must say I did not see that prior to its tabling-he indicated in recommendation 2: "That the federal government reaffirm its commitment to the guarantees in the Canada Health Act to Canadians for a health care system that is universal, accessible, comprehensive, portable and delivered by public and private means and free of user fees or extra billing, et cetera".
Recommendation 1 of the whole report states that the federal government, in co-operation with the provincial and territorial governments, develop a clearly stated national policy on health care that is consistent with the existing Canada Health Act. Those principles are stated in the Canada Health Act.
A second example indicates: "The other major weakness of the report is that it does not put enough emphasis on the responsibility of the federal government for health promotion, protection, disease prevention and medical research".
Recommendation No. 3 of the total report states that the federal government emphasize illness prevention and health promotion, and devote greater resources to education, information, et cetera.
I wish I could discuss this at length. I can assure all my colleagues that a careful reading of the report, particularly the above-noted parts, will show mainly differences in wording but concurrence in essence and substance. Perhaps we could have persuaded him to change his mind and issue a minority report, but since I did not see his minority report I could not have known what he wrote, his claim in it and his position.

Finally, I would like to present a crucial piece of evidence, the Minutes and Proceedings of June 12, at which time the member for Surrey North and myself among other members were in attendance. Page 122 of the report indicates concurrence and: "It was agreed that the draft report as amended be concurred in". That is in the proceedings of our committee. Shall I say the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applies?
In conclusion, I would just like to say that it is sad for a member or a colleague to use an unfounded allegation against another. It becomes even more sad when a colleague uses unfounded allegation to breach House convention.
Allow me to quote what he said:
This misrepresentation of my position caused me embarrassment
and forced me in order to set the record straight to breach House
conventions and release my minority report at noon.
That was five hours before the report was released and three hours before he raised his question of privilege. He had ample time to raise his question and not breach House conventions. Is he telling the House that two wrongs would make a right?
I trust I have proven to the appreciation of this House that the serious allegations that the member for Surrey North did level against this hon. member speaking were unfounded and, should he wish to pursue his grievance further as to facts, I invite him to bring his case before the standing committee where the matter emanated and where it can properly and more fully be debated.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity that I have had to raise this matter of privilege. It arises from a June 5, 1991 press release from the Canadian Gas Association which I have provided to you. This press release was widely distributed and contains false statements about a committee of this House of which I am a member.
My privilege is partly a question of fact and partly a question of law. It is extremely serious for two reasons. First, the unanimous Standing Committee on the Environment report Out of Balance deals with global warming, an issue the committee concluded is a severe threat to Canada and to the world. Second, the statement contained on page 2 of the Canadian Gas Association press release that the standing committee "has come to agree with Canadian Gas Association statistics" is absolutely false and the Canadian Gas Association has failed to withdraw it despite contact by myself.

September 16, 1991
Routine Proceedings
The committee dealt at length with the discrepancy between statistics and chose on page 56 of our report to print both the World Resources Institute figures and the Canadian Gas Association figures with a recommendation for an urgent investigation of Canadian Gas Association data through an independent survey.
This is an extremely serious issue because the Canadian Gas Association claimed to be less than 10 per cent of anthropogenic emissions in Canada, whereas the World Resources Institute, even though it has since reduced its estimate, is listed in our report as being 30 per cent of emissions, methane being a very serious contributor.
I believe this is a question of privilege, and I therefore move that this matter be placed before the appropriate committee, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Election, for consideration.
Although, the chair of the committee is not present today, in his letter to me there is one paragraph that sums up the difficulty that all members of the committee have encountered in this situation regarding methane release. I quote from the letter of July 17 to me from the member for Rosedale, our committee chair:
From that letter the CGA wrote a draft press release and sent me a copy. I was greatly disturbed by the wording of the release and immediately contacted the CGA to voice my disapproval. They agreed to accept suggestions for changes and incorporated them into yet another draft release.
Again I voiced my disapproval with the very negative tone of the press release and the strong language used to to describe the negligence of the committee. I was so disturbed that I informed the association that I would surely go public with our own version of how the WRI data was used and why. It was sure to be very different from the CGA report.
One final note from the paragraph on the second page:
I tried to make it clear to the CGA that the committee's report report was not misleading as their release indicated, and that we nor the CGA were aware until our report came out that WRI had published a retraction on its figures.
I close with that. I believe it is a serious matter, because the CGA press release was widely distributed and there surely is not a more important issue on earth, short of all-out nuclear war, that deserves accurate, forthright information than global warming.

I thank the hon. member for Skeena for bringing the details of this issue to my attention prior to today. I think I should say to hon. members that I have read very carefully the letter the hon. member quoted from the hon. for Rosedale who is the chairperson of the committee in question.
Clearly the hon. member for Skeena and also the chairperson of the committee, the hon. member for Rosedale, are concerned about what happened. The House has heard the facts, but I think the appropriate thing to do at this time is to raise the matter at the very earliest convenience at the committee. After that is done, I may be able to deal with the matter further.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation in Dixon Entrance is now such that there is a real potential for a life threatening incident. Canadian fishing vessels are being boarded by armed U.S. military personnel inside Canada. The vessels are being seized, on-board cargo stolen, Canadian crews are being threatened, assaulted, kidnapped and jailed and ransom payments are being demanded without trial.
This is not a matter that can be dealt with during any of the regular proceedings, as we learned during Question Period today. It is a genuine emergency because a Canadian vessel could be seized at any moment and a growing number of Canadian skippers have expressed the view that their vessels will not be boarded inside Canada by any U.S. authorities. Firearms are present and visible now on Canadian vessels and as I can personally attest, they are visible, present and shown by the U.S military vessels marauding along the A-B line.
This situation in terms of the vessels that were seized and boarded during July and August has not been dealt with by any of the ministers or any of the departments in
Canada. There have been no charges proceeded with or laid against the U.S. authorities for coming inside Canada and committing violations both found within the Criminal Code and that are contrary to international law. Even the Lewis Reef, a Canadian enforcement vessel, that approached the U.S. Coast Guard Liberty when it had the Eliza Joye in custody was refused the right to board the vessel.

The hon. member has raised a matter of some importance. I also have to caution the hon. member that it is not appropriate to get into debate. I think I have the facts thoroughly and fully in front of me. It is a very serious matter. I think that all hon. members would consider that it is.
I do not think that it is appropriate at this time to proceed with an emergency debate, to adjourn the business of the House for an emergency debate today. Of course, we will follow with interest the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I too rise requesting an emergency debate as to the steel industry in this country.
The Canadian steel industry is under unprecedented crisis. Since 1987 imported Canadian steel has fallen to 3 per cent of the American steel market, an all-time low, while American imports into Canada have risen from 2.5 per cent to 17 per cent, an all-time high.
Observers attribute this change in the balance of trade to the relatively high Canadian dollar and the political lobbying of American steel producers. Canadian steel producers and their families are suffering. Unless immediate action is taken to reverse this trend, the situation will become totally untenable.
I suggest a debate is urgently required to convince the government to lower the dollar and provide protection against the flood of steel imports, which has risen above 25 per cent. Unless immediate appropriate actions are taken, there is the possibility that there will be no steel industry in this country.

The hon. member of course has given the appropriate notice for the application. This is not the first time that the matter has been raised in the House. I would ask the hon. member to continue raising it and discussing the matter with others in the Chamber.
September 16, 1991

I do not think it would be appropriate to proceed to an emergency debate today.

Mr. Speaker, as my letter to you reported, European and U.S. actions have resulted in depressed world grain prices and the real incomes of Canadian grain and oilseed producers were at record lows this year. Net incomes were at a record low in the crop year just completed a month and a half ago.
Farmers were continually assured by the government that some defence against these international prices would come forth in a third line of defence. The net income shortfall of more than $1 billion has not been addressed by the government. The crop year ended one and a half months ago.
If Parliament cannot debate this, the government seems to have the intention of forgetting about it and letting those huge debts that farm families have piled up continue.

Facts are what I need to have in front of me, and I would ask hon. members to be careful not to stray into debate. There is a reason for that. Under the rules the applicant for an emergency debate can present the case, but other members are not allowed to be recognized to take issue with something that does stray into the question of debate.
The matter is, of course, one of importance and is well understood in this House to be so. However, I point out to the hon. member that there was extensive debate in Question Period today and there may well be in the ensuing number of days in the next week on the issue, which is as I say important, but it would not be appropriate in my view to proceed to an emergency debate tonight.

Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 52 to request that you give consideration to the following.
It has been almost 20 years since Canada ratified International Labour Organization Convention 87. This freedom of association convention of the UN agency establishes the rights of organized labour. In 1987 the ILO reviewed Canadian back-to-work statutes and ruled that public inconveniences resulting from strikes "cannot justify an abridgement of the fundamental rights
guaranteed by convention 87 unless they reach a point where they affect the life, personal safety or health of all or part of the population".
Nearly one-third of the Public Service Alliance of Canada's bargaining unit has been declared essential, Mr. Speaker, and are not on strike. It appears that Canada is close to breaching this important ILO convention by passing legislation to force those non-essential workers back to work. A debate on the international ramifications of this suggested government action is urgently required, Mr. Speaker, to inform the government of its international commitment and the concerns of this House for the continued respect for these intermittent national conventions.

I thank the hon. member for giving notice of the matter which she has raised. Again, it is an important matter, as are these matters usually when there is an application for an emergency debate. It may well be that there will be sufficient opportunity, perhaps today or in the coming days, to raise the matter in full debate in the House.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would seek the indulgence of the House to appeal for positive consideration under Standing Order 52 for an emergency debate.
This involves the fact that the Canadian pink salmon runs are in very large numbers moving through the fishing grounds into the spawning areas in record numbers, and that the processors in British Columbia have refused to buy Canadian fish. They have instead chosen to purchase Alaska surplus pink at very low costs and thereby have deprived the Canadian fishing industry from earning a living on the resource which they have spent so much money and time in developing.
The failure of the processors to buy Canadian resource while buying the American surplus stocks has resulted in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans not providing an adequate opening on the pink salmon runs. This, of course, will harm-and it is happening right now, harming the people in the fishing industry, harming the communities-and could indeed within the next few days harm spawning channels where massive surpluses of pink salmon move on to those channels and disrupt the spawning process for the preceding fish that have gone on.

September 16, 1991
Business of the House
There is an urgent requirement for a debate and some adjudication of this matter and little action to have it considered in any other forum. I would say that if this House were to consider it in a positive fashion that there are options with CIDA, with the food loans that have been proposed for the Soviet Union. These fisheries on Canadian fish could take place, the communities would be protected, the industry would be protected, and indeed an action of the House on this basis, if we moved immediately, would protect the resource for the future.

Again, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this matter. It is certainly a matter on which the Speaker personally has some intimate knowledge, and I recognize its importance. I think there will be ample opportunity to raise it in the next few days.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to request the consideration of the Speaker for the adjournment of the House for an emergency debate pursuant to Standing Order 52.
There can be no issue of greater or more urgent importance to this House than the state of the Canadian economy and the health of that economy. For this economy to once more re-enter a situation in which recessionary conditions are taking place would be one of the worst economic crises that we could face.
Today Statistics Canada released the first important economic indicator for July which shows that manufacturing across the country has declined for the first time after four months of increase. Combined with the significant rise in bankruptcies in July and the increased rate of unemployment for July and August, Canadians have good reason to fear that we are re-entering the recession.

straying well into debate and it may very well be a debate that the House would want to hear.
I recognize the seriousness with which the application is made, but I think under the circumstances there will be opportunity to raise the matters to which the hon. member refers, certainly in Question Period and possibly on designated days. Point of order, Mr. Speaker-

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
